questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked

Tests practical, auditable governance for multi-team clusters beyond image/security gates.

Key Concepts

- Namespace governance with ResourceQuota and LimitRange
- Namespace-scoped RBAC and ServiceAccounts
- Lightweight CI gates using kubectl/yq
- Local validation vs CI parity

Code Example

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do
  kubectl -n "$ns" get resourcequota >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "Missing ResourceQuota in $ns"; exit 1; }
  kubectl -n "$ns" get limitrange >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "Missing LimitRange in $ns"; exit 1; }
  for dep in $(kubectl -n "$ns" get deploy -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name} {/end}'); do
    sa=$(kubectl -n "$ns" get deploy "$dep" -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName}')
    if [ -z "$sa" ]; then echo "Deployment $dep in $ns uses default SA"; exit 1; fi
    kubectl -n "$ns" get rolebinding | grep -q "$sa" || { echo "Missing RBAC for $sa in $ns"; exit 1; }
  done
done
```

Failing manifest

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: team-a
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      name: app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:latest
```

Passing manifest

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: team-a
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: rq
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    limits.cpu: "8"
    requests.memory: 8Gi
    limits.memory: 16Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: lr
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  limits:
  - max:
      cpu: "4"
      memory: 8Gi
    min:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
    default:
      cpu: 500m
      memory: 512Mi
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: sa-team-a
  namespace: team-a
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: sa-team-a-view
  namespace: team-a
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: sa-team-a
  namespace: team-a
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: view
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      name: app
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: sa-team-a
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:1.21
```

Verification

- Locally: run the gate script against your cluster context and verify it fails/passes as expected; inspect output for missing quota/limitrange or RBAC gaps.
- CI: run the same script in a workflow step; ensure failing manifests fail the build and passing manifests pass.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Assess practical use of OPA in Kubernetes, translating security expectations into verifiable policies; tests demonstrate understanding of Pod spec structure.

## Key Concepts
- Rego fundamentals
- PodSpec fields: volumes.hostPath, securityContext.privileged, capabilities
- OPA test framework and unit tests
- Admission testing approaches

## Code Example
```javascript
package kubernetes.admission

deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  some vol in input.request.object.spec.volumes
  vol.hostPath
  msg := "hostPath volumes are forbidden"
}
deny[msg] {
  some c in input.request.object.spec.containers
  c.securityContext.privileged == true
  msg := "privileged containers are forbidden"
}
deny[msg] {
  some c in input.request.object.spec.containers
  some cap in c.securityContext.capabilities.add
  cap == "NET_ADMIN"
  msg := "NET_ADMIN capability is forbidden"
}
```

## Compliant Pod Manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: compliant-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    securityContext:
      privileged: false
      capabilities:
        add: []
  volumes:
  - name: config
    emptyDir: {}
```

## Noncompliant Pod Manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: noncompliant-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    securityContext:
      privileged: true
      capabilities:
        add: ["NET_ADMIN"]
  volumes:
  - name: host-root
    hostPath:
      path: /
```

## Validation Plan
1. Test policy with OPA: `opa test -v policy.rego`
2. Validate compliant pod: `kubectl apply -f compliant.yaml`
3. Verify noncompliant rejection: `kubectl apply -f noncompliant.yaml --dry-run=server`

## Why This Is Asked

Tests end-to-end image provenance across multi-cloud GPU workloads, combining CI, runtime policies, and verification in real-world constraints.

## Key Concepts

- Image provenance, Cosign, Sigstore, reproducible builds
- Kubernetes admission control (Kyverno/OPA)
- Buildx/OCI digests and registry security
- GPU workload constraints and cross-cloud policy

## Code Example

```yaml
# GitHub Actions: build, sign, verify
name: BuildSignVerify
on: [push]
jobs:
  ci:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up QEMU/Buildx
      - name: Build and push
        run: |
          docker buildx create --use
          image=registry.example.com/project/image:${{ github.sha }}
          docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
            -t $image --build-arg BUILDKIT_INLINE_CACHE=1 .
          cosign sign -key cosign.key $image
          docker push $image
      - name: Verify signature
        run: cosign verify -key cosign.pub $image
```

```yaml
# Kyverno policy (example)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-signed-image
spec:
  validationFailureAction: fail
  rules:
  - name: check-cosign-signature
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: [Deployment]
    verifyImages:
    - image: registry.example.com/*
      pattern: "^.+$"
```

```yaml
# Sample failing manifest (unsigned image)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: guest-deploy
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: registry.example.com/project/image:unsigned

```

```yaml

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:

spec:

    metadata:
      annotations:
        build.sha256: "abcdef123456..."
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: registry.example.com/project/image:sha-abcdef
```

- How would you test policy changes across multiple clusters with blue/green deployments?
- What are failure modes if cosign keys rotate or GitOps sync lags?

## Why This Is Asked
This task tests practical CI gating for container hygiene: linting with Hadolint and enforcing image tagging discipline across manifests.

## Key Concepts
- Hadolint integration in GitHub Actions
- YAML parsing to inspect image tags
- Regular expressions for pinning (no latest, no -dev) and clear failure messages
- Practical debugging of lint vs. policy failures

## Code Example
```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci-docker-k8s.yml
name: CI Gate: Dockerfile lint + tag pin
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, master ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ '**' ]
jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hadolint/hadolint-action@v3
        with:
          dockerfile: '**/Dockerfile'
      - name: Check pinned image tags
        run: |
          set -e
          if grep -RIn 'image:.*:.*(latest|dev.*)' manifests || true; then
            echo 'Unpinned image tag detected' ; exit 1;
          fi
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you scale this gate to many repos?
- How would you extend checks for other tag policies (sha256 digests)?

## Why This Question Is Asked
This question evaluates the ability to integrate image provenance with runtime governance in a GPU-driven, multi-tenant Kubernetes environment. It spans CI pipelines, admission controls, and cross-system attestations—core skills for securing production ML platforms.

## Key Concepts
- **Image Provenance**: Using cosign and Rekor to cryptographically verify container image origins
- **SBOM Signing and Verification**: Ensuring software bills of materials are tamper-proof and traceable
- **Central Provenance Store**: A single source of truth for validated digest information
- **Admission Constraints**: Kyverno/OPA policies enforcing GPU type and quota at deploy time

## Code Example
```yaml
# GitHub Actions: Sign, generate SBOM, and attest
name: Gate: image provenance
on: [push]
env:
  REGISTRY: ghcr.io
  IMAGE_NAME: ${{ github.repository }}
  SIGNING_KEY: ${{ secrets.COSIGN_KEY }}

jobs:
  build-sign-attest:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build and push image
        run: |
          docker build -t ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker push ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Install cosign
        uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@v3
      - name: Sign image with cosign
        run: |
          cosign sign --yes --key ${{ env.SIGNING_KEY }} \
            ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Generate and sign SBOM
        run: |
          syft ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }} -o spdx-json=sbom.json
          cosign attest --yes --key ${{ env.SIGNING_KEY }} \
            --type sbom \
            ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Upload to Rekor (automatic with cosign attest)
        run: |
          echo "Rekor entry created automatically during attestation"
      - name: Store central provenance digest
        run: |
          DIGEST=$(docker inspect ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }} \
            --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}')
          echo "${{ github.sha }}:$DIGEST" >> provenance_store.txt
```

```yaml
# Kyverno admission policy
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: image-provenance-gate
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: verify-image-digest
      match:
        resources:
          kinds: [Deployment]
      verifyImages:
        - imageReferences:
            - "ghcr.io/*"
          attestors:
            - entries:
                - keyless:
                    subject: "https://github.com/org/*"
                    issuer: "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
          verifyDigest: true
          required: true
    - name: enforce-gpu-type
      match:
        resources:
          kinds: [Deployment]
      context:
        - name: namespace
          apiCall:
            urlPath: /api/v1/namespaces/{{ request.namespace }}
      preconditions:
        - key: "{{ request.namespace }}"
          operator: NotEquals
          value: "kube-system"
      validate:
        message: "GPU type must match namespace label"
        pattern:
          spec:
            template:
              spec:
                containers:
                  - (resources.limits."nvidia.com/gpu"): "?*"
    - name: enforce-gpu-quota
      match:
        resources:
          kinds: [Deployment]
      validate:
        message: "GPU quota exceeded for namespace"
        deny: |
          {{ exists request.namespace.metadata.labels."gpu-quota" }}
```

## Why This Question Is Asked

This question evaluates a candidate's ability to design enterprise-grade, policy-driven security controls across hybrid Kubernetes environments. It tests practical knowledge of admission controllers, supply chain security, and multi-cloud consistency—skills essential for platform engineers and security architects.

## Key Concepts

### 1. Image Provenance and Digest Pinning
Digest pinning ensures immutable deployments by locking images to specific content-addressable hashes (e.g., `sha256:abc123...`). This prevents supply chain attacks through tag manipulation. The policy requires images to be referenced by digest rather than mutable tags like `latest` or `v1.2.3`.

### 2. Sigstore Attestations
Sigstore provides cryptographic verification of software supply chain provenance. By validating attestations against allowed signers, organizations ensure that only images built and signed by trusted parties can be deployed. This integrates with the Sigstore transparency log for auditability.

### 3. SBOM Validation
Software Bill of Materials (SBOMs) provide a complete inventory of components within an image. Combined with vulnerability scanners like Grype, this enables organizations to enforce baseline security requirements—such as no critical vulnerabilities or specific library versions—before deployment.

### 4. Pod Security Standards
The policy enforces Pod Security Standards by blocking privileged containers, hostNetwork access, and hostPath volumes. These controls prevent container escape scenarios and limit the blast radius of potential compromises.

## Evaluation Criteria

Strong candidates will demonstrate:
- Understanding of OPA Rego syntax and Gatekeeper constraint templates
- Knowledge of Sigstore's keyless signing and verification workflows
- Familiarity with SBOM generation and vulnerability scanning tools
- Ability to design policies that are both restrictive and operationally practical
- Consideration for multi-cloud and on-premises consistency

```yaml
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install cosign
        uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@v3

      - name: Install Helm and Syft
        run: |
          curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash
          curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anchore/syft/main/install.sh | sh

      - name: Render Helm templates
        run: helm template my-app ./chart --values values.yaml --output-dir ./rendered

      - name: Extract image references
        run: |
          grep -rh 'image:' ./rendered | awk '{print $2}' > images.txt

      - name: Generate SBOM with Syft
        run: |
          syft $(cat images.txt) -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json

      - name: Verify image signatures with cosign
        run: |
          COSIGN_PUBLIC_KEY=cosign.pub
          for IMAGE in $(cat images.txt); do
            cosign verify --key $COSIGN_PUBLIC_KEY $IMAGE || exit 1
          done
```

questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to design a practical, policy-driven CI/CD gate for hybrid cloud/edge Kubernetes, focusing on provenance, reproducibility, and runtime enforcement. It mixes static checks in CI with runtime admission controls, using cosign, SBOMs, and a central provenance store.

Key Concepts

- Cosign verification with in-repo public key
- SBOM generation/verification for artifacts
- ProvenanceDigest tied to a central store and manifest cross-check
- Kyverno policy for runtime rejection of unsigned/mismatched provenance
- Minimal GitHub Actions workflow and OPA policy demonstrating end-to-end flow

Code Example

```javascript
name: ci-gate
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: verify cosign
        run: cosign verify -key cosign.pub image:tag
      - name: verify SBOM
        run: bash -lc 'cat sbom.json | jq .'
      - name: provenance check
        run: bash -lc 'grep -q provenanceDigest <manifest.yaml && echo ok'
```

Follow-up Questions

- How would you rotate cosign keys with zero-downtime for edge clusters?
- How would you test this gate against evolving provenance schemas and multi-tenant RBAC?
